title: Permanent Lights vs. Traditional Christmas Lights: An Honest Comparison
metaTitle: Permanent Lights vs Christmas Lights: Honest Guide
metaDescription: Permanent LED track lights vs traditional string Christmas lights vs hiring an installer. Compare cost over time, safety, convenience, and year-round use.

body.text: If you are weighing permanent LED lights against the traditional string lights you hang every December, you are really comparing three different options: buying and putting up seasonal string lights yourself, paying a company to install and remove lights each year, or installing a permanent LED track system once and being done with it. Each makes sense for different people. This guide walks through the honest trade-offs — cost over time, convenience, safety, daytime and nighttime look, year-round use, and durability — so you can decide without the sales pitch.
The three options, briefly

Traditional Christmas lights are the incandescent or LED string strands most of us grew up with. You buy them, clip them to the roofline each season, plug them in, and take them down in January. They are inexpensive to buy and familiar to use.

Hiring a seasonal installer means a crew shows up in the fall, hangs commercial-grade strands custom-cut to your roofline, comes back to take them down, and stores them until next year. You pay for that service every single season.

Permanent LED track lights — sometimes called permanent holiday lighting or soffit lighting — are individual RGBW LED pucks seated in a low-profile aluminum track that mounts under your soffit or along the fascia once. They stay up all year, tuck out of sight, and are controlled from an app. That is the category we build kits and parts for, so we will be upfront about where the trade-offs land.
Cost over time
Up-front price and true long-term cost are two very different numbers, and this is where the comparison gets interesting.

items: Traditional string lights: cheapest to start — often $50 to $200 for enough strands to cover an average home. But strands fail, colours fade, and a single dead bulb can knock out a run, so most people replace some or all of their lights every few years. Add the value of the hours you spend hanging and removing them, plus the odd new extension cord and timer.

Hiring a seasonal installer: in Canada, expect roughly $500 to $1,500+ per season for an average two-storey home, and more for large or complex rooflines. That cost repeats every year with nothing to show for it afterward — you are renting the look.

Permanent LED track: a larger one-time cost for the kit or the professional install. A DIY LED Housing Package covering a typical home is a single purchase; a professional install adds labour once. After that, your only ongoing cost is a few dollars of electricity, because efficient 12V LEDs draw very little.

body.text: The math that matters: if you are currently paying an installer, a permanent system usually pays for itself in about two to four seasons, and everything after that is essentially free lighting you own. Against DIY string lights the payback is slower and driven more by convenience and durability than by pure dollars — but you also stop re-buying strands and stop spending weekends on a ladder.

Rule of thumb: if you hire an installer every year, permanent lights are almost always cheaper within a few seasons. If you happily hang your own string lights and enjoy it, the case for switching is about time and safety more than money.
Convenience and everyday use

This is the gap most people underestimate. String lights are a project twice a year — untangling, testing, climbing, clipping, then reversing all of it in the cold. An installer removes the labour but ties you to their schedule for both install and takedown.

Permanent lights are controlled entirely from your phone. You set warm white for everyday curb appeal, switch to red and green for the holidays, orange for Halloween, red and white for Canada Day, or team colours for game night — all without touching a ladder. Schedules, dimming, and zones mean the lights come on at dusk and off at bedtime on their own.

body.text: Safety

Hanging string lights means repeated trips up a ladder, often on frozen ground, sometimes on a steep or icy roof, frequently by someone who is not a professional. Ladder falls are a genuine and common winter injury. That risk lands on you every season with DIY string lights.

A permanent system is installed once — by you following a straightforward kit process in good weather, or by an installer — and then never touched again. Low-voltage 12V wiring is inherently safer to work with than line-voltage strands and daisy-chained extension cords, and there are no cords running across gutters or through windows once it is in.
How each looks — by day and by night

Nighttime is where string lights have traditionally won on nostalgia, and modern permanent LEDs match or beat them: individually addressable pucks produce crisp, even points of light, true warm white, and millions of colours with effects like chase, fade, and twinkle. Cheaper string strands can look uneven, show hot spots, or mix slightly different bulb tones as they age.

Daytime is where they diverge most. String lights and their clips are visible on your roofline year-round unless you take them down. Permanent track is designed to disappear: the low-profile aluminum channel tucks up under the soffit, and we offer it in four soffit-matched colours so it reads as trim, not as lights. From the street in daylight, most people never notice it is there.
Year-round use

Traditional Christmas lights do one job for a few weeks a year. That is the core limitation. A permanent system earns its keep the other eleven months: everyday warm-white accent lighting for curb appeal and safety, plus a full calendar of holidays and events without buying anything new. Think of it less as Christmas lights and more as architectural lighting that also does Christmas.
Durability and Canadian weather

Seasonal string lights are generally built to a price and are not intended to live outdoors permanently, which is part of why they fade and fail. Permanent track systems are built for the opposite: sealed, weather-rated pucks in aluminum channel designed to handle Ontario winters, UV, and freeze-thaw cycles year after year. Quality kits back that with a warranty — ours carry a five-year warranty — and because the parts are modular, a single component can be swapped rather than replacing an entire strand.
So which should you choose?

Stick with traditional string lights if your budget is tight this year, you only want lights for a few weeks, and you genuinely do not mind the ladder work. Hire a seasonal installer if you want the look without the labour and are comfortable paying for it every year indefinitely. Choose a permanent system if you want to stop paying and climbing every season, want lighting you own that works year-round, and want the payback to arrive within a few years.

faq.q: Are permanent lights cheaper than hiring someone to hang Christmas lights every year?
faq.a: For most Canadian homes, yes — usually within two to four seasons. A seasonal installer typically charges $500 to $1,500+ per year with nothing owned at the end, while a permanent system is a one-time cost. After it pays for itself, your only ongoing expense is a few dollars of electricity.

faq.q: Do permanent LED lights look tacky or noticeable during the day?
faq.a: No. The LEDs sit inside a low-profile aluminum track that tucks under the soffit, and it comes in four soffit-matched colours so it blends in as trim. From the street in daylight, most people cannot tell it is there. It only stands out when it is on at night.

faq.q: Can I use permanent lights for more than Christmas?
faq.a: Yes, and that is the main advantage. Because each puck is full-colour RGBW and app-controlled, one system does everyday warm-white curb appeal plus every holiday and event — Halloween, Canada Day, sports nights, birthdays — with no takedown and nothing new to buy.

faq.q: Will permanent lights survive Canadian winters?
faq.a: Quality permanent systems are built for it. The pucks are weather-sealed and the aluminum channel is designed for UV, snow, and freeze-thaw cycles, so the lights stay up and working year-round. Ours are backed by a five-year warranty, and individual parts can be replaced if ever needed.

faq.q: Is installing a permanent light kit myself realistic?
faq.a: For a comfortable DIY homeowner, yes. Our kits are low-voltage 12V and come with the track, pucks, controller, power supply, and connectors pre-matched for your run, so the work is mounting the track, seating the pucks, and wiring the low-voltage supply. If you would rather not climb the ladder, we offer professional installation across Southwestern Ontario.

faq.q: What is the difference between the DIY kit and buying individual parts?
faq.a: The DIY LED Housing Packages (50 to 200 linear feet) are complete, matched kits — the simplest way to cover a whole home. Buying individual parts from the shop lets you build a custom run or extend an existing system: pucks, track in four colours, WiFi controllers, power supplies, connectors, power-injection cables, and amplifiers.
